strengths: Strong empirical results demonstrating stable performance through 1,000 sequential edits while baselines degrade significantly (Table 1: 0.963 BERTScore on paraphrases vs 0.070-0.882 for baselines)
Well-motivated two geometric properties of LLM representations (Properties 1 and 2) with convincing empirical validation (Figure 1) forming solid foundation for the approach
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (UnKEBench, EditEverything), models (LLaMA, Qwen), and baselines (7 different methods), with systematic ablations and analysis
Substantial practical improvements: 20% of baseline parameters (32.7M vs 180-293M) with 3× additional compression via shared-subspace training while maintaining utility (0.622 MMLU vs 0.633 baseline)
Thorough analysis including layer sensitivity (Figure 3), edit vector visualization (Figure 4), routing scalability (A.5), latency analysis (A.6), and cluster threshold ablations (A.7)
Practical system design: consistency-robust training for paraphrase generalization, query-adaptive routing for lifelong control, and shared-subspace intervention for memory efficiency
Qualitative case studies (A.8) convincingly demonstrate that RILKE produces coherent, correct outputs after 1,000 edits while baselines produce nonsensical or inaccurate outputs
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification: geometric properties are empirically observed but lack explanation. Why do paraphrases concentrate in representation space? First-order Taylor expansion assumes small perturbations, but actual paraphrase distances may exceed this bound; Property 2 shows substantial scatter (R^l-similarity: 0.586-0.751)

Methodological concerns: (1) Using only last-token representation h^{l,i} for entire query is underexplored and may miss information for longer sequences; (2) Routing threshold 0.9 lacks ablation or principled justification; (3) Gaussian perturbation N(0,σ²I) choice not justified; (4) Multiple clustering hyperparameters (τ_sim, s_max, Δ) without principled selection guidance

Scalability limitations: (1) L2 distance routing is O(m·d) and could bottleneck at millions of edits; no timing analysis provided despite scalability claims; (2) Routing accuracy degrades with dataset size (Figure 6: 95%→85%); (3) Trade-off between memory and paraphrase generalization not thoroughly explored (Table 3: 0.963→0.901 BERTScore)

Limited generalization scope: (1) Evaluated only on 7-8B instruction-tuned models; unclear if mid-layer insights generalize to 70B+ models or base models; (2) Knowledge limited to factual/unstructured; behavioral and capability edits untested; (3) EditEverything paraphrases generated by Gemini (proprietary), not manually validated, raising reproducibility concerns

Statistical rigor issues: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run variance reported. Results appear to be single runs. Case studies (A.8) are qualitative cherry-picks without systematic evaluation

Key design choices lack ablation: Routing similarity threshold (0.9) never ablated; perturbation distribution choices not justified; sensitivity to σ and λ_robu not explored; layer selection requires manual tuning per model

Incomplete technical analysis: No discussion of failure modes or when method breaks down; conflict resolution in shared-subspace training for items with divergent edit targets unexplained; assumption that paraphrases activate same module even after large-scale editing needs validation

Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned; hyperparameter documentation incomplete (σ values, λ_robu, specific EasyEdit configurations); some critical implementation details scattered across appendix or missing

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: lifelong knowledge editing for unstructured knowledge in LLMs
Impressive empirical stability across 1000 sequential edits (maintains ~96% paraphrase generalization while baselines degrade to ~1-2%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: two models, two benchmarks, extensive baselines, plus detailed ablations and analysis in appendix
Strong memory efficiency gains (3.2× compression via clustering, 32.7M vs 180-293M parameters for baselines)
Coherent overall system design combining robust training, adaptive routing, and scalable clustering
Good supporting analyses including layer selection study, routing stability at scale, and case studies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components are straightforward (KL regularization, L2-based routing, standard HAC clustering) applied on top of ReFT

Weak theoretical justification: 'Properties' are empirical observations lacking explanation of why they hold or how they enable lifelong learning; first-order approximation in Eq. 2 has no error analysis
Router design issues: simple nearest-neighbor approach is brittle, threshold of 0.9 unjustified, failure modes not discussed, equidistant query handling not addressed
Significant clustering trade-offs: Table 7 shows 3.5% paraphrase accuracy drop when lowering similarity threshold, but this precision-efficiency trade-off is under-emphasized
No human evaluation: BERTScore/RougeL alone insufficient to validate semantic correctness of edits; suspicious perfect 1.0 scores raise concerns about metric bias

Limited model and data diversity: only two mid-sized models tested (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-7B); paraphrases generated externally by Gemini without detailed description; only MMLU for general utility assessment

Unfair baseline comparisons: FT-L and LoRA perform terribly because they weren't designed for this setting; different parameter budgets across methods (representation vs. weight space) make comparison problematic
Reproducibility concerns: no code release, critical hyperparameters unjustified (σ in noise, λ_robu, 4×4096 rank), Gemini paraphrase generation non-reproducible
Overstated scalability claims: only tested to 1000 edits and 1500 items; no analysis of failure points or scaling beyond current regime
Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite stochastic nature; no ablation on ReFT baseline directly

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem—lifelong editing of unstructured knowledge in LLMs—with a principled representation-space perspective that is well-motivated and clearly presented

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across two models, multiple benchmarks, diverse edit counts (1-1,000), and extensive ablation studies demonstrating consistent superior performance over strong baselines

Strong empirical results achieving near-perfect edit success (1.000) and robust paraphrase generalization (0.963) at scale while preserving general utility and requiring 3-10× fewer parameters than baselines
Identifies and empirically validates two geometric properties of LLM representations that ground the approach and provide interpretable design principles for lifelong editing

Technical contributions are well-executed with proper justification: consistency-robust training via principled first-order expansion, query-adaptive routing, and memory-efficient shared-subspace clustering
Thorough analytical work including ablations on robustness loss, layer selection, clustering thresholds, routing stability, and latency—demonstrating careful engineering and validation
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is limited—the work primarily combines existing techniques (ReFT base, standard KL regularization, nearest-neighbor routing, HAC clustering) without deep conceptual advances. The mechanism for why representation-space interventions mitigate catastrophic forgetting lacks formal analysis

Evaluation relies primarily on semantic similarity metrics (BERTScore, RougeL) rather than direct factual correctness assessment, and thus may not capture hallucinations or subtle errors. No human evaluation or fact-checking validation provided

Property validation is limited in scope: Property 1 shown only for layer 15 of one model; Property 2 demonstrates correlation but not clear causation, and the effect of joint training on alignment is not isolated

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: O(m) routing cost per query with no discussion of efficient indexing for millions of edits; the critical 0.9 similarity gating threshold is under-explored and appears arbitrary

Cluster-shared training reveals significant precision-efficiency tradeoff—paraphrase generalization drops 6% (0.963→0.901)—without deep investigation of cluster quality effects or optimal clustering strategy selection (why HAC vs. alternatives)

Out-of-distribution paraphrase generation (via Gemini for EditEverything) may not reflect robustness to natural paraphrases; low MMLU preservation (0.622 for Llama, 0.712 for Qwen) raises questions about utility retention claims
Missing failure case analysis: no investigation of conflicting/contradictory edits, types of knowledge resistant to editing, routing error modes, or interdependent knowledge modification

Incomplete comparisons: no evaluation against other representation-based methods beyond ReFT, simpler alternatives (prompt-based editing), or baselines with comparable parameter budgets; limited theoretical discussion of when representation-space is fundamentally superior

strengths: Novel representation-space approach to lifelong knowledge editing for unstructured knowledge, with two well-motivated geometric properties (semantic locality and semantic alignment) empirically validated through comprehensive analysis

Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple models and datasets, maintaining stable performance at 1,000 sequential edits while baselines degrade (0.963 BertScore vs. 0.673 for WISE on UnKE), with superior paraphrase generalization and MMLU preservation

Comprehensive method design flowing logically from identified properties: consistency-robust training for generalization, query-adaptive routing for lifelong control, and shared-subspace interventions for memory efficiency (~70% storage savings)

Extensive ablations and analysis including editing distance validation of Prop. 2 (91/100 cases), hyperparameter sensitivity studies, scalability analysis at 1,500 items with >95% routing accuracy, and case studies demonstrating advantages over collapsed baselines
Practical efficiency with 50% memory reduction vs. UnKE baselines and negligible inference latency overhead while maintaining competitive performance across ZsRE structured editing task
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification beyond empirical validation: Properties 1-2 are observed but lack formal explanation; first-order Taylor approximation validity and error bounds in Sec. 4.1 are not analyzed; no formal router correctness analysis

Experimental design concerns that warrant investigation: extremely low temperature (0.001) fundamentally changes task difficulty vs. realistic settings—sensitivity analysis critical but missing; EditEverything paraphrases generated by Gemini introducing potential distribution shift; unclear if baselines evaluated on same synthetic paraphrases

Routing mechanism has unanalyzed failure modes: hardcoded threshold τ_sim=0.9 with limited justification; O(m) lookup cost becomes problematic at scale; no analysis of when nearest-neighbor assumption breaks down in crowded representation spaces; missing error case analysis

Clustering strategy is somewhat ad-hoc: hierarchical agglomerative clustering with recursive refinement lacks theoretical grounding; cluster representations computed once but may shift with accumulating edits; max cluster size s_max=16 appears arbitrary; no comparison with alternative clustering approaches

Scalability limitations not adequately addressed: method requires storing m query representations (O(m·d) memory overhead); indexing becomes problematic at scale; acknowledged limitation of scaling to 'extra-large' knowledge bases but not addressed; true large-scale applicability (10K+ edits) unexplored

Safety and security analysis deferred despite being critical for knowledge editing: acknowledges risks (adversarial edits, bias amplification, robustness to biased policies) in Sec. 9 but defers investigation; concerning given knowledge editing's inherent modification of model behavior

Incomplete empirical validation: no statistical significance testing or error bars; results appear to be single runs; missing sensitivity to temperature parameter despite using extreme value (0.001); paraphrase generation method may introduce artifacts; routing accuracy under uncertainty near threshold not analyzed

Missing comparisons and ablations: no benchmarking against RAG approaches (mentioned but not compared); incomplete comparison with concurrent methods; different clustering strategies not explored; only 2 case studies in appendix; locality claims (1-1% MMLU drop) could use more detailed analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical importance for deployed LLMs; comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, datasets, and baselines with impressive quantitative results (near-perfect performance maintained at 1000 edits while competitors collapse)

Strong empirical validation of the two geometric properties (semantic locality and subspace alignment) with convincing evidence including hard negative analysis; practical efficiency gains are substantial (29.4 vs 224 MiB storage)
Sound technical execution with clear methodology, extensive ablations on layer selection, epsilon, and clustering thresholds; good appendix documentation supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components are incremental extensions of ReFT (consistency regularization via KL divergence, simple cosine similarity routing, standard HAC clustering); no architectural innovations

Weak theoretical justification: Properties 1-2 are purely empirical observations without theoretical grounding; first-order Taylor expansion in §4.1 is informal with unjustified design choices (why ε-ball? why KL divergence on outputs?)

Evaluation concerns: baselines (UnKE, AnyEdit) not designed for 1000-edit lifelong settings; out-of-distribution paraphrases generated synthetically by Gemini; no human evaluation despite only using automatic metrics (BertScore, ROUGE-L); knowledge scope limited to biographical facts

Router design is simplistic and scalability unclear: accuracy drops below 90% on individual items at 1500 edits (Fig. 6); threshold τ_sim=0.9 appears arbitrary; inference latency with many stored representations unexplored; failure modes with conflicting edits unaddressed

Shared-subspace trade-offs understated: Table 3 shows significant generalization drop (0.963→0.901 BertScore, ~6 points); Table 10 reveals substantial performance variance across clustering thresholds; introduces additional hyperparameter without clear tuning guidance

Critical practical considerations unresolved: how edits are specified/validated, user experience with 1000s of active edits, inference behavior at ~95% routing accuracy, conflict resolution for same-entity edits, inference memory requirements for representation indices

Safety and failure analysis deferred: Section 9 postpones adversarial robustness, bias propagation, and robustness under biased policies; only two cherry-picked case studies without error distribution analysis; unclear when semantic locality assumption breaks

Hyperparameter complexity and generalization: many tunable parameters (rank, learning rate, layer, ε, τ_sim) with configuration appearing optimized for specific datasets; unclear guidance for new domains; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

strengths: Well-motivated approach with two clearly identified and empirically validated geometric properties of representation space that provide principled guidance for the method design

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (LLaMA, Qwen), datasets (UnKE, EditEverything, ZsRE), and baselines, with clear demonstration of maintaining stable performance through 1,000 sequential edits while preserving general utility
Significant practical efficiency gains: 3× memory compression over baseline RILKE configuration, ~43% of WISE method, with minimal inference overhead (<1%)
Thorough ablation studies and analysis sections (Tables 3-4, Figures 3-6, Appendix A.6-A.7) that systematically validate design choices and demonstrate scalability up to 1,500 items
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective visualizations and reproducible experimental details; addresses important problem of lifelong knowledge editing for unstructured content
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (consistency training via KL divergence, similarity-based routing, hierarchical clustering) are standard techniques; primary contribution is their combination rather than fundamentally new methods

Theoretical justification for Properties 1-2 is lacking: empirically validated but missing principled explanation of why these geometric properties hold, and unclear whether they generalize beyond these specific datasets/models

Characterization of 'unstructured knowledge' is unclear: datasets still present knowledge as query-answer pairs (essentially structured facts with longer answers), not truly unstructured knowledge like reasoning patterns or procedural knowledge

Router design choices appear arbitrary with limited justification: similarity threshold 0.9 is empirically set; O(m) matching cost at inference scales linearly; Figure 6 shows accuracy dropping to ~90% in individual-mode at scale; scalability beyond 1,500 items unexplored

Precision-efficiency trade-offs in clustering inadequately addressed: Table 10 shows loose clusters (efficiency gain) significantly hurt generalization (0.918→0.883); no principled threshold selection method; missing comparison with alternative clustering approaches
Perfect BertScores (1.0) on training queries (Table 1) raise concerns about potential data leakage or evaluation artifacts; phenomenon not discussed

Risk analysis deferred to future work (adversarial edits, bias propagation): acknowledged limitation but significant gap for knowledge editing work; even preliminary analysis would strengthen contribution

Limited evaluation scope: only instruction-tuned models tested; EditEverything uses synthetic Gemini-generated paraphrases rather than human variants; limited comparison with recent baselines; underlying assumption that paraphrases fall within ε-ball lacks rigorous justification
